evidence.title: The Effect of Ambient Listening Technology on the Patient Experience
evidence.outcome: Patient-reported satisfaction across six domains with vs without ambient scribe use
evidence.effect: Ambient scribe use associated with higher odds of satisfaction with perceived time spent with provider (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01-1.26, p=0.033); no detectable differences in other domains.
evidence.quote: Patients whose provider used an ambient scribe had higher odds of reporting satisfaction with the perceived duration of time spent with the provider (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.01-1.26, p = 0.033).

evidence.title: Effect of use of ambient listening technology on patient-reported communication and satisfaction ratings
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Patient-reported communication and satisfaction ratings after AI scribe deployment, pilot vs control physicians (difference-in-differences)
evidence.effect: Pre-post change in communication and satisfaction scores did not differ significantly between pilot and control physicians; three items rose for pilot physicians and declined for controls without reaching significance.
evidence.quote: The pre-post change in communication and satisfaction scores did not differ significantly between pilot and control physicians.

evidence.title: Large-Scale Implementation of Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation and Its Effects on Electronic Health Record Efficiency and Clinician Well-Being
evidence.outcome: Clinician satisfaction, intent to remain, and work-life balance surveyed post-deployment
evidence.effect: Survey (n=233; 26.4% response rate) at 45 days post-activation showed improved satisfaction, work-life balance, and strong preference to continue using DAX.
evidence.quote: Survey responses (n = 233; 26.4% response rate) indicated improvements across domains, with most respondents reporting reduced burnout, increased job satisfaction, improved work-life balance, and a strong preference to continue using DAX.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Scribes on Clinical Workflow and Documentation Quality: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: Patient perceptions of AI scribe use
evidence.effect: Patients were not negatively affected by AI scribe use and the vast majority found it helpful (no numbers given in abstract).
evidence.quote: Patients were not negatively affected by using an AI scribe, and the vast majority found it helpful.

evidence.title: Patient and dermatologists' perspectives on augmented intelligence for melanoma screening: A prospective study
evidence.venue: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
evidence.effect: Augmented intelligence induced a significantly higher feeling of safety than AI or dermatologist screening alone.
evidence.quote: Regarding SSS, AuI induced a significantly higher feeling of safety than AI (mean-SSS (mSSS): 9.5 vs. 7.7, p < 0.0001) or dermatologist screening alone (mSSS: 9.5 vs. 9.1, p = 0.001).

evidence.title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe Among Clinicians and Patients: Real-World Prospective Observational Time-Motion Study
evidence.outcome: Patient acceptance and comfort after consultations using the ambient scribe
evidence.effect: 27 of 39 surveyed patients (69.2%) agreed their physician focused on them more during the consultation; none expressed discomfort with the technology.
evidence.quote: Patient acceptance was favorable: of 39 surveyed patients, 27 (69.2%) agreed that their physician focused on them more during the consultation, and none expressed discomfort with the technology.

evidence.title: Ambient AI Documentation and Patient Satisfaction in Outpatient Care: Retrospective Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Patient satisfaction and experience after ambient AI scribe deployment
evidence.effect: Patient satisfaction scores increased across all three items after DAX implementation (0.9 to 1.9 points); only the concern item was significant (P=.01).
evidence.quote: Aggregate scores for individual items increased between 0.9 and 1.9 points.

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.effect: Clients reported frustration due to a lack of communication and emotional support during the rapid scan encounters.
evidence.quote: Clients expressed frustration with the lack of communication and support.

evidence.title: Ambient AI Scribe Implementation in an Ambulatory Setting in a Single Medical Group: Prospective Study
evidence.outcome: Patient experience ('provider listened to me' satisfaction scores) after ambient AI use
evidence.effect: No significant effect on patient satisfaction scores (P=.39).
evidence.quote: Patient experience, as measured by "provider listened to me" scores on patient satisfaction surveys, was not significantly affected by ambient AI use (P=.39).

commentary.bottom_line: Three deployment studies in the United States show that post-deployment surveys of patients and clinicians can be run and can register small differences, such as an odds ratio of 1.13 for perceived time with the provider, but none compared surveying with not surveying, measured trust directly, or tracked patient opt-out rates. The evidence speaks more to the feasibility of the practice than to its value in catching eroded trust.

perspectives.view: Two quasi-experimental studies (8120 and 31917 patient surveys) and one pre-post clinician survey used post-deployment surveys to measure the effects of AI scribes. None tested whether surveying detects harm or changes decisions, and none tracked opt-out rates. Findings were mixed and the outcomes are indirect for this practice, so certainty is very low.

Across two patient studies, surveys found one small difference (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01-1.26) and otherwise no detectable change. Surveys may therefore miss erosion of trust unless shifts are large. A Sierra Leone study found client frustration during rapid AI-assisted scans, which shows the problem can occur but does not show that surveys catch it.

The clinician survey had a 26.4% response rate at 45 days after activation, so its reported gains in satisfaction and work-life balance may reflect the views of those who chose to respond. The patient studies drew on existing post-visit survey programs, which suggests the practice can fit current workflows where experience data are already collected.

All three tests took place in the United States and did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The only study in a limited English and rural population, from Sierra Leone, documented patient frustration with AI-assisted encounters. Written surveys may miss such patients unless they are offered in other languages and formats.

The two patient studies analyzed 8120 and 31917 surveys, which suggests health systems can reuse existing patient experience instruments at scale. Detecting small effects required these large samples and a control group of physicians. No study reported the cost or staff time needed to run surveys or track opt-outs.

No study measured how often patients declined AI use or whether they could reach a human instead. Most hazard studies found no harm to patient experience, including a randomized trial of 279 patients. The Sierra Leone study reported frustration from a lack of communication and emotional support. Opt-out tracking remains untested as a signal of patient trust.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without structured post-deployment surveys, measured trust as a distinct construct, or tracked patient opt-out rates as an early warning signal. Studies are needed that test whether survey and opt-out signals lead to timely changes in how AI is used, and that report response rates by language, insurance type, and literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three studies testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one study in a limited English and rural population documented the hazard but did not test surveying, so the value of this practice for underserved patients is unknown.
